Design comparison · for sign-off

Material Design, drawn three ways

The same page of the running platform, built three times: as it ships today, with the palette layer generated by Material 3’s colour engine, and with M3’s language on top of that. Nothing here is a drawing — every picture is a real build of Mobile’s Plan page.

Drawn from v3.22, byte-identical baseline Viewport 1440×900 Method three builds, same sources Date 2026-09-06

What is already Material about SMP

The architecture M3 recommends is the one _shared.css already draws: Layer 1 the language (type scale, shape, weight — never themed), Layer 2 the palette (colour only, four blocks). Those are M3’s reference and system token layers under different names. So this is not “adopt a system”; it is “change where the values come from”.

  • Today9,132 lines of CSS across nine files, 834 classes, ~2,790 rules, 41 colour tokens per palette block.
  • Shape6 / 8 / 12 / 16 / pill, against M3’s 4 / 8 / 12 / 16 / 28 / full.
  • Colourthe --good / --good-tx / --good-bg trio is M3’s primary / on-primary-container / primary-container by another name.
  • Brandingtwo colours in, eight tokens out, derived in sRGB. M3 takes one seed and produces every role, in HCT.

Level 1 — the colour engine

Every value in the palette layer becomes a tone on a tonal palette, computed in HCT from two seeds that are the house’s own: the navy bar and the gold accent. The four status hues keep their own hue and chroma, so On track stays green and Off track stays red in every brand.

Primary — the navy bar
Tertiary — the gold accent
Neutral — every surface
Neutral variant — lines and quiet ink

HCT rather than OKLCH or LCh(ab), and it matters here specifically: both of those shift hue as lightness changes, worst in the blues — which is exactly where SMP’s navy lives. The implementation reproduces Google’s own baseline exactly: seeded with #6750A4, tone 40 lands on #6750A4 byte-for-byte and the other five reference tones are within 1.

Level 1 moves nothing structural, and that is measured rather than claimed: the pane, the rail, the table, the tab row and the first six row heights are identical to the pixel at all three widths.

The test that actually matters

On the house’s own seeds the generated palette reproduces what was hand-tuned over ten versions — 12 of 15 sampled tokens move, by a handful of points each, and the page looks the same. That is the finding, not a disappointment: the hand-tuning was good, and the generator agrees with it.

So the question Level 1 answers is not how it looks for Raya Trade. It is what happens for a brand nobody has tuned by hand — every client after the first. Below, the same tenant (deep purple bar, warm sand accent) rebranded through the product’s own Setup › Branding path, and then with those same two colours used as seeds.

Build

Today’s branding moves 8 of the 41 tokens in a palette block. The other 33 stay as they were — including --stone, which on this purple-branded tenant is still #16325C, Forefront’s own navy. Level 1 derives the neutrals from the seed’s hue, so the greys carry the brand instead of arguing with it, and all 44 contrast pairs still clear for a colour nobody checked.

Level 2 — the language

Shape to M3’s corner scale, sentence case in place of tracked uppercase, tonal containers in place of hairlines, and a state layer on every interactive thing. This is where Material stops being a colour system and becomes recognisable.

The trade is visible in the picture and it is the thing to argue about: M3 has no data-table component at all, and its nearest surface is a pale header on surface-container. Adopting it takes the tenant’s brand colour off every table head in the product — which reverses §41.10, where that colour was put there deliberately.

Three costs found by building it rather than reasoning about it

  • Specificity§41.10 enforced the table head with !important at .scroll table thead th, so a plain thead th !important provably matches and provably does nothing. The pale header cannot be added — the existing declaration has to be edited.
  • State layerthe naive one-rule version introduces 14 new contrast failures on small type in the rail. M3’s state layer is not a rule you append; it needs per-control work.
  • ShapeM3’s pill radius belongs to buttons. Applied to every <button> it hits the pillar rail’s rows, which are buttons, and the rail comes out as a stack of arcs.

Density turned out not to be the problem I expected: even with M3’s shape and type, row heights are unchanged and nothing overruns its pane at 1100px. The blocker is the state layer and the table head, not the row height.

Level 3 — Material Web components. Not viable.

Worth saying plainly so it is not revisited: @material/web ships as npm ES modules needing a bundler, and package.json deliberately has no build script; the product is one self-contained HTML file that must open from file://; the CSP is default-src 'self' with a build-time hashed script-src. And the components use Shadow DOM, which breaks the data-fld binding model, every elementFromPoint probe, the contrast sweep and clipTitles().

What is possible is drawing SMP’s own controls to M3’s specs by hand, surface by surface — a per-screen mockup exercise, not a switch.

Level 1

Recommended

Generate the palette from seeds. Token names unchanged, zero structural movement, the sweep stays clean, and tenant branding becomes provably legible instead of checked-and-reported. It leaves Levels 2 and 3 open.

Level 2

Second, and separable

Worth taking for the state layer alone — it would close §16.17, where every hover and focus colour in the product is an unmeasured one-off. But it needs the 14 failures above solved per control, and it asks you to give up the brand colour on every table head.

Level 3

Ruled out

Not by preference — by the single-file, no-bundler, hashed-CSP constraints the product is built on.

What I need from you

  1. Level 1 — yes or no? If yes it is a real change to _shared.css plus ~200 lines of colour maths inlined into the build, and every colour value in the product shifts by a few points. Nothing on any screen moves.
  2. The identity question. Material is strongly recognisable as Google’s. Level 1 is invisible on that axis; Level 2 is not — a consulting product wearing pill buttons and sentence-case labels reads as assembled from Google’s kit. That is a positioning call, not a technical one.
  3. The table head. If Level 2 is ever on the table, this reverses §41.10. Worth knowing now whether that is even acceptable, because it is most of what Material would take away.
